lines.speaker: Minos
lines.text: This robber here, Sostratus, is to be thrown into Pyriphlegethon. The temple-robber is to be torn apart by the Chimera. And the tyrant, Hermes—stretch him out next to Tityus and let the vultures take a turn at his liver too. As for you good people, off with you, quickly, to the Elysian Field. Take up residence in the Isles of the Blessed, in return for the decent things you did while alive.

lines.speaker: Sostratus
lines.text: Hear me out, Minos. See if what I say sounds fair.

lines.speaker: Minos
lines.text: I have to hear you again? Sostratus, haven't you been fully exposed as a villain—and a man who murdered all those people?

lines.speaker: Sostratus
lines.text: Exposed, yes. But consider whether I should fairly be punished.

lines.speaker: Minos
lines.text: Quite fairly, if it is fair to pay the penalty one deserves.

lines.speaker: Sostratus
lines.text: Still, answer me this, Minos. It is a short question.

lines.speaker: Minos
lines.text: Go on. Only keep it short. We do have the rest of the docket.

lines.speaker: Sostratus
lines.text: Everything I did in life—did I do it of my own will, or had it been spun for me by Fate?

lines.speaker: Sostratus
lines.text: Then all the respectable people, and we who are called villains, were doing these things as her servants?

lines.speaker: Minos
lines.text: Yes. Servants of Clotho, who assigned each man at birth what he was to do.

lines.speaker: Sostratus
lines.text: Now suppose someone, compelled by another person, kills a man and cannot contradict the one forcing him—an executioner, say, or a bodyguard: one obeying a judge, the other a tyrant. Whom do you blame for the killing?

lines.speaker: Minos
lines.text: Plainly the judge or the tyrant. We do not blame the sword either. It is an instrument; it serves the anger of the person who first supplied the cause.

lines.speaker: Sostratus
lines.text: Excellent, Minos. Very generous of you to improve my example. Now if a man arrives carrying gold or silver because his master sent him, whom do we thank? Whom do we list as the benefactor?

lines.speaker: Minos
lines.text: The sender, Sostratus. The man who carried it was only the courier.

lines.speaker: Sostratus
lines.text: Then you see how unjustly you are acting: punishing us, who were servants of Clotho's orders, and rewarding these people for having carried out someone else's good deeds. No one can seriously say it was possible to refuse commands issued under total necessity.

lines.speaker: Minos
lines.text: Sostratus, if you examined things too closely, you would find a great many arrangements down here that make no rational sense. Still, you shall get the benefit of that question, since you seem to be not only a robber but something of a sophist. Hermes, release him. No more punishment. But see that you don't teach the other dead to ask the same thing.
